title: Feather stitch
subtitle: Alternating angled chain loops that build a branching line
excerpt: Feather stitch alternates open chain loops to the left and right of a central line, producing a branching feather-like column suited to smocking panels and botanical borders.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), feather stitch entry.
heroPrompt: Feather stitch column running vertically on cream cotton, alternating loops to either side, 2-strand thread, close-up, natural light.

content.text: Feather stitch is an open fly stitch alternated left and right. Each loop tilts to one side, is anchored at its tip, and the next loop starts from that anchor and tilts to the other side. The result is a chain of V-shapes that zigzags down a central line.
Draw a centre line. Bring the needle up on the line at the top.
Insert the needle to the right of the line and slightly lower, bring it up on the line below the insertion point, thread under needle. Pull through to form the right-leaning loop.
Now insert the needle to the left of the line and bring it up on the line again. Thread under needle. Pull through to form the left-leaning loop.
Continue alternating left and right down the line. Keep loop sizes and angles consistent.

items.symptom: The column drifts to one side
items.cause: Loops on one side are larger than the other.
items.fix: Check the width of each loop against the centre line before moving on. Equal width on each side keeps the column straight.

items.cause: Loops are varying sizes or the anchor points are not on the centre line.
items.fix: Work on drawn guide lines until the rhythm is established.

content.text: Feather stitch is standard in smocking, where it joins pleats. Double feather stitch adds a second loop to each side for a more elaborate branch. Both are common in Crazy patchwork seam decoration.
